title: Transition from children's to adult services (NICE NG43)
blurb: Plan a young person's move to adult services in line with NICE NG43: when to start, who coordinates, how to involve them and what to do if they disengage.
question: Jordan, 12, has cystic fibrosis and is in Year 7. His mother asks when the team should start planning his move to adult services. What does NICE NG43 recommend?

teach.body: Moving from children's to adult services is a risky time: young people can disengage and their health can worsen. Formally, NICE NG43 defines transition as the purposeful, planned process of supporting young people to move to adults' services, and transfer as the point at which responsibility passes. Plain English: start early, plan with the young person as an equal partner, give them one named person to coordinate, and make sure someone follows them up afterwards.
teach.cite: NICE NG43 Transition from children's to adults' services (2016)

items.label: Named worker support begins at least
At relative stability, not a rigid age
Named worker support continues at least

teach.caption: Young people entering a service close to transfer start planning immediately; care leavers from age 15½.

teach.body: Transition support should fit the young person's maturity, cognitive abilities, psychological status, long-term conditions, circumstances, caring roles and communication needs (1.1.2). It should be strengths-based, treat them as an equal partner, build their confidence to direct their own care, and cover education and employment, community inclusion, health and wellbeing, and independent living (1.1.3–1.1.4).

letters.word: Engage the GP and primary care
Duration: at least 6 months each side

teach.caption: Could be a nurse, youth worker, AHP, the named GP or an existing keyworker. Hands over to someone in adults' services.
No specialist adult service? Involving the GP is 'absolutely critical' (1.3.9).

teach.h: Involving parents, respecting the young person

rows.label: Ask how they want parents involved

teach.note: Capacity is considered under the Mental Capacity Act principles where relevant.

children.label: Adult services follow up
children.sub: Contact them and family; involve GP

children.label: Review the care plan
children.sub: Find another way to meet needs

teach.caption: Same adult practitioner for the first 2 attended appointments after transfer (1.4.4).

teach.text: Transfer should not happen just because the young person has turned 16 or 18. NG43 1.2.3 says the point of transfer should not be based on a rigid age threshold and should take place at a time of relative stability, for example not in the middle of exams or a flare of their condition.

teach.body: Leah has juvenile idiopathic arthritis. Her mother always answers for her. Nurse Daniel asks Leah how she would like her mother involved, then offers part of the appointment for Leah on her own to raise questions. He checks how she manages her medicines, agrees goals with her for school and independence, and updates her transition plan, which is reviewed at least annually.

items: Start planning from Year 9 (13–14) at the latest; immediately if close to transfer.
Review the transition plan at least annually, with the young person and GP involved.
One named worker, at least 6 months before and after transfer, then handover.
Transfer at relative stability, not a rigid age; meet adult staff first.
If they disengage, adult services follow up and refer back to the named worker.

summary: You can now plan a developmentally appropriate transition that starts by Year 9, is coordinated by a named worker and involves the young person as an equal partner. You can also respond when a young person disengages after transfer, in line with NG43.

A.q: Jordan, 12, has cystic fibrosis and is in Year 7. His mother asks when the team should start planning his move to adult services. What does NG43 recommend?
options: From Year 9 (13–14) at the latest
At 16, when he can consent
Six months before his 18th birthday
When he leaves school
A.why: NG43 1.2.1: start planning for adulthood from Year 9 (age 13 or 14) at the latest.

whyNot.1: Sixteen is later than the Year 9 starting point.
whyNot.2: Six months before 18 is far too late for planning to start.
whyNot.3: Leaving school is not the trigger; planning starts by Year 9.

A.q: Ben, 15, has epilepsy and sees a different nurse at almost every clinic. He is preparing to move to adult services. What does NG43 recommend to coordinate his transition?
options: A rota of clinic nurses
The adult consultant from now on
His parents as coordinators
A single named worker
A.why: NG43 1.2.5: help the young person identify a single practitioner to act as a named worker coordinating transition.

whyNot.0: A rota does not give one person with a meaningful relationship.
whyNot.1: The named worker coordinates; adult practitioners meet him before transfer.
whyNot.2: Parents are involved, but a practitioner coordinates.

A.q: How often should a young person's transition plan be reviewed under NG43?
options: Every 3 years
Every 5 years
At least annually
At the point of transfer
A.why: NG43 1.2.4: hold an annual meeting to review transition planning, or more often if needed.

whyNot.3: Reviews happen throughout transition, at least yearly.

B.q: Leah, 16, has juvenile idiopathic arthritis. At clinic her mother always answers for her. What does NG43 suggest?
options: Ask her mother to wait outside every time
Offer Leah time to raise concerns on her own
Continue as her mother knows her best
Delay transition until Leah speaks up
B.why: NG43 1.2.21: give young people the chance to raise concerns and queries separately from their parents, and ask how they would like their parents involved.

whyNot.0: Leah's preference about her mother's involvement should be asked, not a blanket rule imposed.
whyNot.2: This does not build Leah's confidence to direct her own care.
whyNot.3: Delaying transition does not help her develop independence.

B.q: Aisha, 17, has type 1 diabetes. She is due to move to the adult clinic next month but has just had two admissions with DKA and is starting exams. What should the team consider?
options: Transfer as planned, as the date is set
Transfer early so adults manage the DKA
Transfer at a time of relative stability
Discharge her to the GP instead
B.why: NG43 1.2.3: the point of transfer should not be based on a rigid age threshold and should take place at a time of relative stability.

whyNot.0: A fixed date should not override her current instability.
whyNot.3: Discharge to the GP is not a substitute for planned specialist transfer.

B.q: Ravi, 17, has a rare metabolic condition. The children's team want to reduce his anxiety about moving to the adult service. Which step does NG43 recommend before transfer?
options: Arrange for him to meet an adult practitioner
Send his notes by post to the adult team
Tell him the adult team will be the same
Let him find the clinic on his first visit
B.why: NG43 1.3.1: a practitioner from adult services should meet the young person before transfer, for example through joint appointments or clinics.

whyNot.1: Sharing notes is needed but does not prepare Ravi himself.
whyNot.2: Giving inaccurate reassurance is not appropriate.
whyNot.3: Visiting adult services beforehand is recommended (1.3.6).

C.q: Ellie, 18, moved to the adult cystic fibrosis service three months ago and has missed her last two appointments. What should happen first under NG43?
options: Discharge her back to the GP
Refer her back to the children's team
Wait for her to re-refer herself
Adult services try to contact and follow her up
C.why: NG43 1.4.1: if a young person does not attend after transfer, adult services, within safeguarding protocols, should try to contact them and their family, follow them up and involve the GP.

whyNot.1: Referral back is to the named worker, after follow-up and assessment.
whyNot.2: Passive waiting does not meet the follow-up recommendation.

C.q: Tom, 17, has complex needs and does not meet the criteria for any specialist adult health service. What does NG43 emphasise?
options: Keep him in children's services indefinitely
Involving his GP in transition is critical
Close his case when he turns 18
Transfer him to an adult ward for review
C.why: NG43 1.3.9: if a young person does not meet the criteria for specialist adult health services, involving the GP in transition planning is absolutely critical. Signpost non-statutory support too.

whyNot.0: Staying indefinitely in children's services is not the plan.
whyNot.2: Closing the case leaves him without support.
whyNot.3: An adult ward admission is not a transition plan.

C.q: Sara, 16, has congenital heart disease and will transfer in about a year. Her named worker is a children's nurse. For how long should the named worker support her?
options: Until the day of transfer
For 4 weeks after transfer
At least 6 months before and after transfer
Until her first adult appointment
C.why: NG43 1.2.9: the named worker supports the young person for at least 6 months before and after transfer, then hands over to someone in adult services.

whyNot.0: Support continues after transfer, not ending on the day.
whyNot.1: Four weeks is shorter than the minimum.
whyNot.3: Support continues beyond the first appointment.

reteach.title: Early, one person, follow through
reteach.question: What three things make a transition safe?

blocks.body: Early: start by Year 9 and review every year. One person: a named worker the young person trusts, for at least 6 months either side of transfer. Follow through: meet adult staff first, transfer when stable, and if they stop attending, adult services follow up and refer back to the named worker.

blocks.text: The 18th birthday is not a transfer plan. NG43 rejects rigid age thresholds.

explain.body: From Year 9 (13 or 14) at the latest; immediately if entering services close to transfer. For care leavers, from 15½. Plans are reviewed at least once a year.

test.q: Marcus, 17, is referred to a children's renal service for the first time, a few months before he would usually transfer. When should transition planning start?
options: Immediately
At 18
In Year 9
After his first adult review
test.why: NG43 1.2.1: for young people entering the service close to the point of transfer, planning should start immediately.

whyNot.3: Planning should come before, not after, adult review.

explain.body: One practitioner with a meaningful relationship coordinates, links with the GP, helps navigate services, supports the family and advocates if needed. At least 6 months before and after transfer, then hands over.

test.q: Who can act as a young person's named worker under NG43?
options: A senior executive in the trust
Their own parent or carer
A receptionist in adult services
A nurse they know and trust
test.why: NG43 1.2.6: the named worker could be a nurse, youth worker, AHP, the named GP or a keyworker, and should be someone with whom the young person has a meaningful relationship.

whyNot.0: A senior executive is accountable for transition strategy (1.5.1), not individual coordination.
whyNot.1: Parents are involved, but the named worker is a practitioner.
whyNot.2: A receptionist is not a practitioner coordinating care.

explain.body: Meet an adult practitioner before transfer, visit adult services, prepare a personal folder (for example 3 months before) and assess readiness to self-manage any long-term condition.

head: Include
rows: Health, education and social care needs
Emergency care plans and admissions history

test.q: Which item does NG43 suggest including in a young person's personal folder for adult services?
options: Their school timetable
Their emergency care plans
Their siblings' records
Their exam results
test.why: NG43 1.3.3 lists emergency care plans among the folder contents, alongside a one-page profile and history of unplanned admissions.

whyNot.0: A school timetable is not a listed item.
whyNot.2: Siblings' records are not part of the young person's folder.
whyNot.3: Exam results are not a listed item; hopes and achievements are.

explain.body: See the same adult practitioner for the first 2 attended appointments. If the young person does not attend, adult services follow up within safeguarding protocols and involve the GP; if they still do not engage, refer back to the named worker.

test.q: After transfer, what continuity does NG43 recommend for adult health appointments?
options: Same practitioner, first 2 visits
A different doctor at each visit
A nurse-led telephone review first
Group clinics from the first visit
test.why: NG43 1.4.4: ensure the young person sees the same practitioner in adult services for the first 2 attended appointments.

whyNot.2: Telephone review is not the continuity recommendation.
whyNot.3: Group clinics are not the recommendation.
